summary: TWZ 获得了有关海狼级潜艇康涅狄格号在 2021 年在南中国海与水下海山相撞后正在进行维修的新细节。海军一直在考虑大约三年的时间表来建造替换的船首声纳导流罩。最终，仅用了不到一年的时间就建成了。康涅狄格州的总体维修计划已被推迟，我们是第一个报告该船预计要到明年夏天才能恢复使用的人。编者注：这篇报道发表后，Janicki Industries 达成了
content:
TWZ 获得了有关海狼级潜艇康涅狄格号在 2021 年在南中国海与水下海山相撞后正在进行维修的新细节。海军一直在考虑大约三年的时间表来建造替换的船首声纳导流罩。最终，仅用了不到一年的时间就建成了。康涅狄格州的总体维修计划已被推迟，我们是第一个报告该船预计要到明年夏天才能恢复使用的人。编者注：这篇报道发表后，Janicki Industries 联系我们，要求在进行额外审查时删除圆顶的图像。出于礼貌，我们同意了，如果完全获得批准，我们将重新发布它。 Janicki Industries 今天告诉我们，该公司在大约 10 个月内生产出了新型船首声纳导流罩，并于 2024 年交付给海军。据其网站称，Janicki 拥有为美国核潜艇项目生产“声纳罩和精密加工硬件”的历史。它还支持各种备受瞩目的航空航天项目，包括 B-21 袭击者轰炸机和 F-35 联合攻击战斗机。根据一份经过大量编辑的海军事故报告，康涅狄格号的船头在五年前的碰撞事件发生后，最初至少在某种程度上仍然保持着连接状态。然而，当潜艇一瘸一拐地驶向关岛时，整个船首结构随后断裂。
随后，这艘船驶往加利福尼亚州圣地亚哥，然后前往华盛顿州的普吉特海湾海军造船厂和中间维护设施 (PSNS-IMF)，此后一直待在那里。 2023 年，在普吉特湾海军造船厂和中间维护设施中看到的康涅狄格号航空母舰，其船首圆顶明显缺失。美国海军“普吉特海湾海军造船厂和国际货币基金组织（中间维护设施）需要按照船的计划，在其后面没有生产线的情况下安装一个精密的替换圆顶，”贾尼基在撰写本文时还在其网站上表示。 “Janicki 比次佳选择快了 24 个月，因为工作所需的一切都集中在一个屋檐下：适合半球的 5 轴铣床、证明这一点的计量方法以及形成双曲板的 1,000 吨压力机。”本文顶部的部分图片和下面的完整图片显示了 Janicki 专有的五轴铣床在圆顶上工作的情况。海狼级潜艇艏声纳导流罩的尺寸和复杂性怎么强调都不为过。这些船上的船首声纳阵列直径为 24 英尺。圆顶本身的结构必须按照非常严格的规格建造，以使声纳系统正常工作。海狼级潜艇上的艏声纳阵列，其艏穹顶被拆除。公共领域 过去的五角大楼预算文件和国会拨款法案已经强调了更换康涅狄格州弓形声纳罩的预期成本和复杂性。
2021 年，立法者批准了 1000 万美元专门用于圆顶的资金，以及 4000 万美元用于其他“紧急维修”。全部维修费用仍不得而知，但预计将远高于 5000 万美元。 在 2024 年发布的 2025 财年预算提案中，海军还概述了购买额外船首圆顶的计划，以防其任何一艘“海狼”级潜艇再次遭受类似的严重事故。 “海狼级潜艇的保障战略不包括提供替换潜艇

【原文 English Original】
TWZ has obtained new details about the ongoing repairs to the Seawolf class submarine USS Connecticut following collision with an underwater seamount in the South China Sea in 2021. The Navy had been looking at a roughly three-year timeline for the construction of a replacement bow sonar dome. In the end, it took just under a year for it to be built. The overall schedule for repairs to Connecticut has suffered delays, and we were the first to report that the boat is now not expected to return to service until next summer. Editor’s note: After this story was published, Janicki Industries reached out to us to ask that the image of the dome be taken down while an additional review is conducted. Out of courtesy, we agreed, and we will repost it if and when it is fully approved. Janicki Industries produced the new bow sonar dome in approximately 10 months and delivered it to the Navy in 2024, the company told us today. Janicki has a history of producing “sonar domes and precision machined hardware” for U.S. nuclear submarine programs, according to its website . It has also supported various high-profile aerospace programs, including the B-21 Raider bomber and F-35 Joint Strike Fighter . Connecticut ’s bow had initially remained attached, at least to some degree, following the collision five years ago, according to a heavily redacted Navy report on the accident . However, the entire bow structure subsequently broke away as the submarine limped to Guam . The boat then sailed to San Diego, California , and then to the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard & Intermediate Maintenance Facility (PSNS-IMF) in Washington State, where it has been ever since. USS Connecticut seen at the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard & Intermediate Maintenance Facility in 2023 with its bow dome prominently missing. USN “Puget Sound Naval Shipyard & IMF [Intermediate Maintenance Facility] needed a precision replacement dome with no production line behind it, on the boat’s schedule,” Janicki also says on its website at the time of writing . “Janicki delivered it 24 months faster than the next-best option because everything the job needed sits under one roof: 5-axis mills that fit a hemisphere, the metrology to prove it, and the 1,000-ton press that forms double-curved plate.” The picture seen in part at the top of this story and in full below shows one of Janicki’s proprietary five-axis milling machines at work on the dome. The size and complexity of the bow sonar dome on Seawolf class submarines cannot be overstated. The bow sonar arrays on these boats is 24 feet in diameter. The structure of the dome itself has to be built to very exacting specifications for the sonar system to work properly. A look at the bow sonar array on a Seawolf class submarine with its bow dome removed. Public Domain Past Pentagon budget documents and appropriations bills from Congress had already highlighted the expected costs and complexities of replacing Connecticut ’s bow sonar dome. In 2021, lawmakers approved $10 million in funding specifically for the dome, as well as $40 million for other “emergent repairs.” The full repair bill is still unknown, but is expected to be far steeper than just $50 million. In its Fiscal Year 2025 budget proposal , released in 2024, the Navy also outlined plans to acquire an additional bow dome in case any of its Seawolf class submarines suffered another similarly severe mishap. “The Seawolf Class submarines sustainment strategy did not include the provisioning of replacement bow domes; therefore, no replacement bow domes for these in-service submarines are within the Navy’s inventory,” the budget documents explained. “This program would procure one Seawolf Class bow dome for use in the event replacement is required. Funds in FY25 are to purchase a bow dome which has a three plus year lead time.” Note here the mention of a lead time of at least three years, which is in line with Janicki’s statement that the “next-best option” would have taken two years more to do this work. As TWZ has highlighted in years of reporting now, repairs to Connecticut , in general, were always set to be challenging and costly due to the small size of the Seawolf class and the design being long out of production. The Navy originally planned to acquire 29 of these boats, but ultimately bought just three as a result of post-Cold War drawdowns. In addition, shrinking the program of record so severely caused the unit price of each one to rise substantially, just over $10 billion in 2025 dollars. At the time of writing, they are still the most costly attack submarines ever built. The last of the Seawolf class submarines, the highly secretive USS Jimmy Carter , which entered service in 2005, is also a heavily modified sub-type optimized for underwater espionage missions . USS Connecticut at sea in 2009. USN It is also worth noting that the U.S. Navy, as well as some of its foreign counterparts , have repaired similarly severe damage to submarines by cannibalizing entire sections from decommissioned boats in the same class. However, this is not an option given the size of the Seawolf class and the still very high demand for them operationally . The core design offers advanced capabilities that make even USS Seawolf and USS Connecticut especially well suited to a variety of specialized tasks . This is clearly why the Navy has continued to invest so much in returning Connecticut to the fleet. As mentioned, repairs to Connecticut are now not expected to be finished until sometime in the summer of next year. This is the latest in a succession of schedule slips in recent years. The original goal had been for the boat to be back in service by September 2025. “The Navy’s target completion date for the availability is the summer of 2027. PSNS & IMF is dedicated to executing this work with the highest standards of safety, technical accuracy, and craftsmanship to ensure the ship returns to the fleet ready to take its place at the tip of the spear in defense of our nation’s interests,” a Navy official told TWZ in September. “Current work consists of structural and systems restoration and required lifecycle maintenance.” Earlier in the year, the Navy also revealed that it is now planning on sending Connecticut into retirement in 2031. This means the submarine has just four more years of service ahead of it if the current repair schedule holds. The Navy does have plans to acquire a new class of nuclear attack submarines, currently referred to as SSN(X). In the past, the service has described those future boats as more of a direct successor to the Seawolf class than the versions of the Virginia class it is buying now. A picture of the first-in-class USS Seawolf . USN “The analytical conclusion was unequivocal: to dominate high-end peer threats in the middle of this century, a clean sheet design is required. The Virginia class is a fantastic, unmatched world-class warship, and it will remain the backbone of our attack fleet for decades,” Navy Rear Adm. Andrew Miller said at the Naval Submarine League’s main annual conference last week, per USNI News . “As adversary capabilities evolve, we require expanded payload capacity, greater electrical and hydrodynamic margins and unprecedented architectural flexibility that simply cannot be backfitted into an existing hull form.” Miller is currently the head of the Undersea Warfare Division with the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations. In terms of desired key capabilities for SSN(X), the Navy wants “first, higher flank speed and tactical control speed. Two, improved operational availability. Three, decisive lethality. Four, superior stealth and layered survivability, and finally organic robotic and autonomous systems hosting and command and control,” Miller added. “We are redefining the role of the submarine from a standalone hunter-killer to a capital mothership. By launching uncrewed systems directly from submarine torpedo tubes and integrating unmanned [robotic] vehicles into our battle plans, we dramatically expand the tactical reach of our manned fleet.” The first SSN(X) submarines are not expected to begin entering service until the mid-2040s, at the earliest. The Navy will continue acquiring Virginia class submarines in the interim. This includes stretched Block IV and V versions with Virginia Payload Modules (VPM) that will now be categorized as guided-missile types (SSGN). There will also be a one-of-a-kind seabed warfare version of the Virginia , which could well take over for the USS Jimmy Carter. A briefing slide from General Dynamics Electric Boat detailing existing and future planned subvariants of the Virginia class nuclear submarine. The Block VI and V types have now been reclassified as nuclear-powered guided missile submarines (SSGN) rather than nuclear-powered attack submarines (SSN). General Dynamics Electric Boat When it comes to USS Connecticut , if there are no further delays, the fully repaired submarine with its new bow sonar dome should be back in service by the middle of next year. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post New Bow Sonar Dome For Heavily Damaged Submarine USS Connecticut Seen For The First Time (Updated) appeared first on TWZ .

title: USS Theodore Roosevelt Now in the Middle East, Lincoln’s Last Escorts Finally Home
zh_title: 西奥多·罗斯福号航空母舰现已抵达中东，林肯最后的护航终于回家
summary: 2026 年 11 月 15 日，西奥多·罗斯福号航空母舰 (CVN-71) 穿越印度洋。作为计划部署的一部分，该航母目前正在美国中央司令部责任区执行任务。美国海军照片 美国第三艘航空母舰及其护航舰现已抵达中东。周日，西奥多·罗斯福号航空母舰 (CVN-71) 切入美国第五舰队。随着美国和伊朗之间的紧张局势持续存在，西奥多·罗斯福号航母打击群的到来使美国在中东地区出现了三个航母打击群。周末，胡塞武装继续占领巴布埃尔附近地区。
content:
2026 年 11 月 15 日，西奥多·罗斯福号航空母舰 (CVN-71) 穿越印度洋。作为计划部署的一部分，该航母目前正在美国中央司令部责任区执行任务。美国海军照片 美国第三艘航空母舰及其护航舰现已抵达中东。周日，西奥多·罗斯福号航空母舰 (CVN-71) 切入美国第五舰队。随着美国和伊朗之间的紧张局势持续存在，西奥多·罗斯福号航母打击群的到来使美国在中东地区出现了三个航母打击群。周末，胡塞武装继续对曼德海峡（连接亚丁湾与红海的战略要道）周围地区提出主权要求，而伊朗军队则声称他们周五袭击了位于巴林的美国雷达。美国中央司令部否认了社交媒体网站 X 上发布的有关伊斯兰革命卫队在巴林发射两架单向无人机并被击落的说法。 2026 年 11 月 16 日，美国水兵在尼米兹级航空母舰西奥多·罗斯福号 (CVN-71) 的飞行甲板上使用分配给第 8 直升机海上作战中队 (HSC) 的 MH-60S 海鹰进行飞行作业。西奥多·罗斯福号被部署到美国第五舰队作战区域，以支持中东的海上安全与稳定。美国海军照片 西奥多·罗斯福预计将接替 8 月底抵达中东的乔治·华盛顿号航空母舰 (CVN-73)。
虽然 GW 最终接替了亚伯拉罕·林肯号航空母舰 (CVN-72)，但在安倍回国之前，这两艘航母都与乔治·H·W·布什号航空母舰 (CVN-77) 一起在中东执行任务大约一个月。目前还不清楚随着 TR 的到来，GW 将在该地区停留多久。布什、GW和TR在中东的存在是以美国航母在印太地区的存在为代价的。安倍在部署 321 天后启程回国，而其两艘护航舰——迈克尔·墨菲号 (DDG-112) 和斯普鲁恩斯号 (DDG-111)——则留在了后方。迈克尔·墨菲 (Michael Murphy) 在服役 346 天后于周四返回家中，而斯普鲁恩斯 (Spruance) 在服役 357 天后于周六返回家中。斯普鲁恩斯的部署时间比安倍多了 36 天，创下了驱逐舰部署的记录。阿利·伯克级导弹驱逐舰斯普鲁恩斯号 (DDG-111) 于 2026 年 11 月 13 日返回圣地亚哥海军基地母港，结束了在美国第 3、第 7 和第 5 舰队作战区域为期 12 个月的战斗部署。美国海军照片 对于驱逐舰来说，长达近一年的部署是罕见的，它们通常会部署六到七个月。然而，海军警告水手和家属，随着海上服务试图满足政府的需求，部署将持续近一年。斯普鲁恩斯于 2025 年 11 月 21 日从加利福尼亚州圣地亚哥海军基地部署。
据海军发布的宣布该驱逐舰回归的消息称，该驱逐舰在第三、第五和第七舰队中服役，在整个部署过程中航行了超过 88,000 海里。 2026 年 11 月 13 日，海军水手和亲人欢迎阿利·伯克级导弹驱逐舰斯普鲁恩斯号 (DDG-111) 返回其母港圣地亚哥海军基地，结束了在美国第三、第七和第五舰队行动区为期 12 个月的战斗部署。美国海军照片 斯普鲁恩斯号在部署期间参与了史诗狂怒行动，在此期间，作为持续海上封锁的一部分，驱逐舰禁用了货船 M/V Touska。虽然新闻稿称该舰发射了战斧导弹，但没有详细说明

【原文 English Original】
USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) transits the Indian Ocean, Nov. 15, 2026. The aircraft carrier is currently operating in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility as part of a scheduled deployment. US Navy photo A third U.S. aircraft carrier and its escorts are now in the Middle East. USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) chopped into U.S. 5th Fleet on Sunday. The arrival of the Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group makes three U.S. carrier strike groups in the Middle East, as tensions persist between the U.S. and Iran. Over the weekend, the Houthis continued to claim areas around the Bab el-Mandeb – the strategic chokepoint that connects the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea – while Iranian forces claim they attacked a U.S. radar in Bahrain on Friday. U.S. Central Command denied the claim posting on social media site X that the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps launched two one-way drones at Bahrain, which were shot down. U.S. sailors conduct flight operations with an MH-60S Sea Hawk assigned to Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron (HSC) 8 on the flight deck of Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71), Nov. 16, 2026. Theodore Roosevelt is deployed to the U.S. 5th Fleet area of operations to support maritime security and stability in the Middle East. US Navy photo Theodore Roosevelt is expected to relieve USS George Washington (CVN-73), which arrived in the Middle East toward the end of August . While GW ultimately relieved USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72), the two carriers both operated in the Middle East, along with USS George H.W. Bush (CVN-77), for about a month before Abe headed home. It is unclear how long GW will stay in the area with TR’s arrival. Bush , GW and TR’s presence in the Middle East comes at the cost of the U.S. carrier presence in the Indo-Pacific region. While Abe headed home after 321 days on deployment, two of its escorts – USS Michael Murphy (DDG-112) and USS Spruance (DDG-111) – stayed behind. Michael Murphy returned home Thursday after 346 days deployed, while Spruance returned home on Saturday after 357 days deployed. Spruance’s deployment came in at 36 days more than Abe and set a record for destroyer deployments. Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Spruance (DDG-111) returns to its home port of Naval Base San Diego, Nov. 13, 2026, concluding a 12-month combat deployment across the U.S. 3rd, 7th, and 5th fleet areas of operations. US Navy photo Nearly year-long deployments are rare for destroyers, which usually go out for six to seven months. However, the Navy has warned sailors and families to expect deployments that approach a year as the sea service attempts to keep up the needs of the administration. Spruance deployed on Nov. 21, 2025, from Naval Base San Diego, Calif. The destroyer operated in the 3rd, 5th and 7th fleets, traveling more than 88,000 nautical miles throughout its deployments, according to a Navy release announcing the destroyer’s return. U.S. Navy sailors and loved ones welcome Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Spruance (DDG-111) as it returns to its home port of Naval Base San Diego, Nov. 13, 2026, concluding a 12-month combat deployment across the U.S. 3rd, 7th, and 5th fleet areas of operations. US Navy photo While deployed, Spruance was part of Operation Epic Fury, during which the destroyer disabled cargo vessel M/V Touska as part of the ongoing maritime blockade. While the release said the ship launched Tomahawk missiles, it did not go into details about the Iranian military targets. The destroyer did take out 12 drones and four anti-ship cruise missiles while in the Middle East, according to the Navy release. The “Raptors” of HSM-71 embarked on Spruance and flew 190 sorties during the deployment, reads the release. Spruance received the Presidential Unit Citation and Combat Action Ribbon following its role in Operation Epic Fury. The destroyer has been busy over the past two years. Before its most recent deployment, the ship was part of U.S. Northern Command’s southern border operations, leaving San Diego in March 2025. Prior to that, Spruance spent five months in the Middle East as part of the U.S. response to Houthi attacks on commercial shipping, coming home on Dec. 19, 2024.

title: Navy Weapons Division to Make Tomahawk Components in 2027
zh_title: 海军武器部门将于 2027 年生产战斧部件
summary: 2026 年 2 月 28 日，阿利·伯克级导弹驱逐舰小弗兰克·E·彼得森号 (DDG-121) 在支持史诗狂怒行动的行动中发射战斧对地攻击导弹。美国海军照片 海军空战中心武器部门上周宣布，将于 2027 年 6 月开始制造战斧巡航导弹弹头的组件，届时一种新型炸药和推进剂混合器上线。 11 月 9 日，由 B&P Littleford 制造的新型 300 加仑搅拌机在加利福尼亚州中国湖推进实验室举行剪彩仪式。一旦混音器上线
content:
2026 年 2 月 28 日，阿利·伯克级导弹驱逐舰小弗兰克·E·彼得森号 (DDG-121) 在支持史诗狂怒行动的行动中发射战斧对地攻击导弹。美国海军照片 海军空战中心武器部门上周宣布，将于 2027 年 6 月开始制造战斧巡航导弹弹头的组件，届时一种新型炸药和推进剂混合器上线。 11 月 9 日，由 B&P Littleford 制造的新型 300 加仑搅拌机在加利福尼亚州中国湖推进实验室举行剪彩仪式。 NAWCD 在一份新闻稿中表示，一旦混合器上线，NAWCD 的弹头生产团队将努力在制造商雷神公司需要弹头之前准备好弹头，帮助确保连续、准时地将战斧交付给舰队。 8月，海军授予雷神公司一份价值229亿美元的合同，以加速战斧生产，目标是每年生产1000多枚导弹。在“史诗狂怒行动”之后，国防部一直在努力增加和加速导弹和弹药的生产，该行动导致弹药迅速消耗。五角大楼的努力还集中于扩大制造商和供应商的国防工业基础，建设产能和冗余。 2026 年 11 月 9 日，来宾聚集在大型混合湾，观看中国湖推进实验室剪彩后新型 300 加仑混合机的演示。
一旦在 2027 年 6 月左右上线，混合器将使海军空战中心武器部门的能量团队达到为舰队生产战斧弹头的生产率。美国海军照片推进和能量部门负责人瑞安·亨特在新闻稿中表示，更快的生产需要更大的弹头容量。中国湖的海军实验室和马里兰州海军水面作战中心印度司令部表示，他们可以进行弹头的生产工作。目前，雷神公司是战斧制造的主要承包商，而通用动力军械和战术系统公司负责加工弹头箱，而 L3Harris 则为其装载炸药。 9 月，L3Harris 和 NAWCWD 签署了一项多年的公私合作伙伴关系，以制造导弹部件。亨特说，根据该协议，NAWCWD 计划生产部分战斧弹头。一年前，当 NAWCD 能源团队从博物馆取出一个战斧弹头盒时，NAWCD 开始了拥有制造战斧弹头能力的过程。能源团队将炸药和火箭推进剂混合在一起，并将其装入海军武器中。 2026 年 11 月 9 日，中国湖推进实验室大型混合舱中，新型 300 加仑行星混合器的叶片位于混合碗上方。该混合器将于 2027 年 6 月左右投入使用，将使海军空战中心武器部门的能量团队达到舰队战斧弹头的生产率。
美国海军照片 该团队清理了箱子并混合了 PBXN-107 炸药并填充了 WDU-36/B 弹头。测试、成像和 X 射线证实该团队正确填充了它。经过这一努力，今年秋天，同一个团队填充了七个首件战斧弹头，这是新生产商建造的第一批用于检查的装置。能量处理部门负责人赞恩·戈德特表示，一旦通过，它们将成为“中国湖”的第一批生产弹头。弹头由中国湖运行了数十年的 150 加仑混合器填充，新的混合器将取代它。在演示构建过程中，团队还发现

Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. (DDG-121) fires a Tomahawk Land Attack Missile during operations in support of Operation Epic Fury, Feb. 28, 2026. US Navy photo The Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division will begin making a component for Tomahawk cruise missile warheads in June of 2027 when a new explosive and propellant mixer comes online, the division announced last week. A new 300 gallon mixer, built by B&P Littleford was inaugurated in a ribbon cutting ceremony on Nov. 9 at the China Lake Propulsion Laboratory in California. Once the mixer is online, NAWCD’s warhead production team will work to have warheads ready before manufacturer Raytheon needs them, helping ensure continuous, on-time Tomahawk deliveries to the fleet, NAWCD said in a news release . In August, the Navy awarded Raytheon a $22.9 billion contract to accelerate Tomahawk production with a target of producing more than 1,000 missiles annually. The Department of Defense has been carrying out efforts to increase and accelerate productions of missiles and munitions following Operation Epic Fury, which has seen munitions rapidly expended. Pentagon efforts have also focused on expanding the defense industrial base of manufacturers and suppliers, building both capacity and redundancy. Guests gather in the large mix bay to watch a demonstration of a new 300-gallon mixer after its ribbon cutting at the China Lake Propulsion Laboratory, Nov. 9, 2026. Once online around June 2027, the mixer will let Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division’s energetics team reach production rate on Tomahawk warheads for the fleet. US Navy photo Faster production calls for more warhead capacity, said Ryan Hunter, head of the Propulsion and Energetics Division, in the release. Navy labs at China Lake and at Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division in Maryland said they could do the work to produce warheads. Currently, Raytheon is the prime contractor building Tomahawks while General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems machines the warhead cases and L3Harris loads them with explosives. In September, L3Harris and NAWCWD signed a multi-year public-private partnership to manufacture missile components. Under it, Hunter said, NAWCWD plans to produce a portion of the Tomahawk warheads. NAWCD began the process of having the capability to build Tomahawk warheads a year ago when the NAWCD energetics team pulled a Tomahawk warhead case out of a museum. The energetics team mixes explosives and rocket propellants and loads them into Navy weapons. The blades of a new 300-gallon planetary mixer rest above the mix bowl in the large mix bay at the China Lake Propulsion Laboratory, Nov. 9, 2026. Once online around June 2027, the mixer will let Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division’s energetics team reach production rate on Tomahawk warheads for the fleet. US Navy photo The team cleaned the case and mixed PBXN-107 explosive and filled the WDU-36/B warhead. Testing, imaging and X-rays confirmed the team filled it correctly. Following that effort, this fall, the same team filled seven first-article Tomahawk warheads, the first units a new producer builds for inspection. Once they pass, they become China Lake’s first production warheads, said Zane Goedert, head of the Energetics Processing Branch. The warhead was filled by a 150-gallon mixer China Lake has run for decades, which the new mixer will replace. During the demonstration build, the team also found the warhead specification needed a major update. Key parts and materials to address the issue can take up to a year to arrive, reads the NAWCD release. Patricia Hottowe, director of the Tomahawk Technical Project Office at NAWCWD, said in the release that the team spent much of the past year updating the specification and the approved supplier list. The Navy’s technical authority for the warhead must approve each new supplier and every future producer – Navy or industry – must build to that specification. NAWCWD also bought long-lead materials ahead of the multi-year contract, Hottowe said. A dozen new personnel have been hired to join the team, Goedert said. They will train under experienced technicians on safety, quality and procedures for about a year before working on their own. He added that loading the warhead is the easiest part while buying materials, bringing on people and getting answers are harder. Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Delbert D. Black (DDG-119) fires a Tomahawk Land Attack Missile (TLAM) in support of Operation Epic Fury, Feb. 28, 2026. US Navy photo The branch has filled warheads for the AGM-84H/K Stand-off Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (SLAM-E) missile since the mid-1990s. Goedert said his team routinely turns one-of-a-kind prototypes around on short timelines. That experience allowed the team to move faster on Tomahawk. According to Hunter, the challenge comes from a system built for fixed multi-year schedules. Now that system must move faster on a shorter clock. China Lake’s facilities will be able to meet that challenge due to its layout. “Because our plant is dispersed and because we will be curing the warheads in a different area than we’re casting them, we’re able to do simultaneous processes that will get higher throughput,” said Hunter. The plant’s newest buildings grew out of a rebuild as the July 2019 earthquakes destroyed three energetics compounds in the Salt Wells area of the China Lake Propulsion Laboratory, reads the release. Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command broke ground on their replacements, known as the trio, in April of 2022. Goedert said the team designed the Motor Assembly Compound to cut handling. Large rocket motors risk damage each time crews move them after casting. The same layout will speed warhead work. Rear Adm. Eric Gardner, principal deputy for the Portfolio Acquisition Executive Munitions, spoke at the ribbon cutting and said the first-article warheads will lay the groundwork for China Lake to become an additional source of Tomahawk warhead production. “At PAE Munitions, we know that increasing weapons production takes more than contracts and funding,” Gardner said. “It takes people, infrastructure, materials, and strong partnerships across our Navy, our warfare centers and industry.”

title: The Nvidia Scandal Exposes American Blind Spots
zh_title: 英伟达丑闻暴露美国盲点
summary: 华盛顿已经建立了一个复杂的出口管制和许可要求网络，以防止人工智能芯片进入中国。然而，英伟达创始人黄仁勋与被指控向北京传递信息的中国女商人黄爱丽之间明显的“美人计”事件，不仅仅是这些控制措施的盲点问题。它讲述了在全球化、互联的世界中关闭先进技术的困难，以及一家公司、监管机构和行政部门看到了警告信号却迟迟未采取行动。如果现有规则得到执行，Nvidia
content:
华盛顿已经建立了一个复杂的出口管制和许可要求网络，以防止人工智能芯片进入中国。然而，英伟达创始人黄仁勋与被指控向北京传递信息的中国女商人黄爱丽之间明显的“美人计”事件，不仅仅是这些控制措施的盲点问题。它讲述了在全球化、互联的世界中关闭先进技术的困难，以及一家公司、监管机构和行政部门看到了警告信号却迟迟未采取行动。如果现有规则得到执行，英伟达就不应该向总部位于新加坡的云计算公司 Megaspeed International 出售先进芯片。 Alice Huang 是 Megaspeed 的高管，该公司成为 Nvidia 的主要客户，并因可能违反美国出口管制而受到审查。英伟达董事会已聘请外部顾问来调查中国情报部门是否针对其前首席执行官，后者在其事务曝光后辞职。该公司坚称，没有理由相信其机密或国家安全受到损害。这个故事的核心是供应链的不透明性，而它始于 Megaspeed 错综复杂的所有权。该公司于2015年在新加坡注册成立，名称为第七大道国际，是中国网络游戏行业中的新兴企业。它于 2023 年采用现名。
同年晚些时候，Megaspeed 的股份通过一家在英属维尔京群岛注册的公司转让给另一家在新加坡注册的公司 Swiftdata。谁最终控制 Swiftdata 目前尚不清楚。错综复杂的注册流程并不能证明国家控制，中国投资也不等同于中国政府所有权。但中国的国有资本和私人资本经常通过子公司、控股公司和离岸工具进行流动。 Megaspeed 复杂的企业历史本应引发严格审查，审查谁控制该公司以及谁最终将从其购买美国芯片中受益。尽管存在警告信号，Megaspeed 仍成为 Nvidia 的官方云合作伙伴，并购买了价值数十亿美元的先进计算设备。其印度尼西亚子公司进口了最先进的 Nvidia 硬件。美国当局已调查Megaspeed是否也帮助中国客户获得Nvidia芯片。 Megaspeed 否认非法转让，也没有任何公开调查结果证实存在出口管制违规行为。但英伟达面临的问题从来不是违规行为是否得到证实；而是问题。问题在于具有这种特征的客户是否值得信任和访问。 2025 年 8 月，Nvidia 总法律顾问通过电子邮件向负责调查 Megaspeed 的部门特工发送电子邮件，称商务部高级官员已批准此次外展活动。调查已暂停并移交给司法部。
其他机构提议将 Megaspeed 添加到被认为对美国国家安全构成风险的外国企业和组织的实体名单中。商务部从未这样做过。官员们敦促商务部采取行动，国务卿马可·卢比奥 (Marco Rubio) 于 2026 年 5 月向商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克 (Howard Lutnick) 发送了一份有关 Megaspeed 的备忘录。据报道，财政部长斯科特·贝森特 (Scott Bessent) 最近与卢特尼克对质，问道：“Megaspeed 为何不在实体名单上？”商务部否认发生过交易。白宫收到警告。据报道，唐纳德·特朗普总统去年年底听取了简报和一份关于爱丽丝的机密备忘录

【原文 English Original】
Washington has built an elaborate web of export controls and licensing requirements to keep artificial intelligence chips from reaching China. Yet Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s apparent “honeytrap” affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of passing information to Beijing, is about more than the blind spots of those controls. It is about the difficulty of shutting down access to advanced tech in a globalized, interconnected world — and about a company, a regulator, and an executive branch that saw warning signs and were slow act on them. Had existing rules been enforced, Nvidia should never have been selling advanced chips to the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International. Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, which became a major Nvidia customer, and attracted scrutin y over possible violations of American export controls. Nvidia’s board has retained outside counsel to investigate whether Chinese intelligence targeted their former CEO, who resigned after his affairs were revealed. The company maintains that it has no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised. At its core, the story is about the opacity of supply chains, and it begins with Megaspeed’s convoluted ownership. The company incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, emerging from the Chinese online gaming industry. It adopted its current name in 2023. Later that year, Megaspeed’s shares were transferred , through a company registered in the British Virgin Islands, to another Singapore-registered company, Swiftdata. Who ultimately controls Swiftdata remains unclear. Convoluted incorporation trails do not prove state control, and Chinese investment is not synonymous with Chinese government ownership. But state-linked and private Chinese capital often  moves  through subsidiaries, holding companies, and offshore vehicles. Megaspeed’s complex corporate history should have triggered rigorous scrutiny of who controlled the firm and who would ultimately benefit from its purchases of US chips.  Despite the warning signs, Megaspeed became an official Nvidia cloud partner and purchased billions of dollars’ worth of advanced computing equipment. Its Indonesian subsidiary imported cutting-edge Nvidia hardware. US authorities have investigated whether Megaspeed also helped Chinese customers obtain Nvidia chips. Megaspeed has denied illicit transfers, and no public finding has established an export-control violation. But the question for Nvidia was never whether a violation had been proven; it was whether a customer with this profile warranted trust and access. In August 2025, Nvidia’s general counsel  emailed  Department agents investigating Megaspeed, saying that a senior Commerce official had approved the outreach. The investigation was paused and transferred to the Justice Department.  Other agencies proposed adding Megaspeed to the entity list of foreign businesses and organizations that are deemed to pose a risk to US national security. Commerce never did. Officials  pressed  Commerce to act, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick a memorandum on Megaspeed in May 2026. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently reportedly  confronted  Lutnik, asking: “How come Megaspeed isn’t on the entities list?” Commerce denies that the  exchange  took place. The White House was warned. President Donald Trump was reportedly briefed late last year and a classified memorandum on Alice Huang circulated among senior officials before his May visit to China. Apparently, no action was taken. Instead, Nvidia CEO Huang joined the presidential delegation to Beijing and, in September, attended the White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping. Jensen Huang’s own conduct compounded the failure. An executive with his access to the president and to sensitive policy discussions carries a responsibility that goes beyond his obligations to shareholders. A relationship with a foreign national linked to a customer under federal investigation was, at best, reckless. Washington depends on companies such as Nvidia to sustain its technological lead over China, expand domestic computing capacity, and support an increasingly AI-dependent defense posture. Yet these companies  remain  commercial enterprises that  are  accountable to shareholders and driven by incentives that might not always align with national security objectives.  Get the Latest Sign up to receive regular Bandwidth emails and stay informed about CEPA's work. Although enforcing existing export controls would have gone a long way to prevent this crisis, the case reveals a genuine gap. US export controls focus on where advanced chips are shipped, yet access to computing power no longer requires owning the hardware.  Renting “offshore” computing is often legal. A Chinese company banned from purchasing certain advanced US processors may be able to buy computing capacity from servers in another jurisdiction. Megaspeed reportedly  provided computing services to Chinese technology customers, including the Chinese e-commerce leader Alibaba. This gap risks widening as AI infrastructure expands across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and other regions. The US needs to enforce existing rules and close the gaps. First, that means applying export controls consistently. When the evidence warrants, enforcement must be separated from corporate lobbying — and acted on. Second, add access to advanced computing power to export controls, not just the chips themselves. That means know- your-customer  requirements for cloud providers and close monitoring of overseas cloud infrastructure. Third, invest in systematic mapping of corporate ownership and financial networks. Screening named entities is insufficient when relationships extend across holding companies, investment vehicles, and multiple jurisdictions. Chipmakers should be expected to know who ultimately owns their customers. Fourth, establish clear security expectations and channels for intelligence-sharing with executives at the commanding heights of American technology. Congress is preparing to act. Top Republican and Democratic lawmakers hope to  include  three proposed measures toughening rules on exporting AI chips. Three House committee chairs have  demanded  a closed-door briefing from Huang.  His resignation should not end the inquiry. Congress should examine not only whether sensitive information was compromised, but how Megaspeed won Nvidia’s trust, why Commerce never acted, and why intelligence warnings to the executive branch failed to translate into meaningful action. The US has spent years building the tools to control what crosses its borders. But tools are only as strong as the institutions that wield them. title: Commerce moves to place new restrictions on sale of AI chips abroad
zh_title: 商务部对人工智能芯片海外销售实施新限制
summary: 美国商务部正急于制定新的出口规则，阻止美国公司利用其他国家的第三方数据中心交易来逃避人工智能芯片销售的限制。周一，工业与安全局宣布了一项长达 132 页的临时最终规则，限制美国芯片制造商向国外第三方数据中心出售人工智能芯片的能力。该规则对出口、再出口和转移到美国武器禁运国家的海外数据中心增加了新的限制。该名单目前涵盖20多个国家，包括中国、古巴、伊朗、
content:
美国商务部正急于制定新的出口规则，阻止美国公司利用其他国家的第三方数据中心交易来逃避人工智能芯片销售的限制。周一，工业与安全局宣布了一项长达 132 页的临时最终规则，限制美国芯片制造商向国外第三方数据中心出售人工智能芯片的能力。该规则对出口、再出口和转移到美国武器禁运国家的海外数据中心增加了新的限制。该名单目前涵盖 20 多个国家，包括中国、古巴、伊朗、利比亚、朝鲜和苏丹。最终临时规则指出：“这些限制将削弱总部位于相关国家的公司使用美国先进的超级智能（SI）半导体来训练先进的 SI 模型的能力。” “数据中心、外国代工厂和芯片出口商必须对其客户进行严格的尽职调查，包括[这些国家]人员的任何直接或间接所有权或控制权，作为遵守这一新控制措施的一部分。”该规则还要求向不在武器禁运名单上的其他五个国家销售先进人工智能芯片需要新的许可证：印度尼西亚、马来西亚、新加坡、泰国和巴西。商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克已确定，这些国家存在芯片被转移到世界其他地区的“高于正常风险”。
即将或正在进行芯片销售的公司有 90 天的时间获得新许可证，其中对海外芯片设计者的豁免将减少。“临时最终”指定允许商务部绕过大部分正常的联邦规则制定程序。根据非营利组织美国行动论坛的说法，这一指定通常是为“紧急情况和其他需要的时候”保留的。商务部援引《2018 年出口管制改革法案》的授权，在不事先通知和发表评论的情况下实施这些变更。美国立法者一直将美国在半导体行业的主导地位视为相对于中国等竞争对手的关键优势，中国正在努力建设自己的国内人工智能芯片行业。一些专家敦促联邦政府进一步收紧此类芯片的全球销售，以防止它们被外国敌对势力转移或购买。将人工智能芯片列入武器禁运清单反映出人们对人工智能系统在黑客攻击和生物武器设计等领域带来的危险日益担忧。该规定是在美国芯片巨头英伟达前首席执行官黄仁勋因与员工和一名中国商业伙伴发生多起婚外情的报道而辞职几天后发布的。这位同事是中国公司 Megaspeed 的 Alice Huang，她作为潜在的中国政府资产而受到美国政策制定者的审查。报道还称，她帮助促成了 Megaspeed 和 Nvidia 之间价值 120 亿美元的人工智能芯片交易，其中一些可能已运往中国。
商务部对人工智能芯片海外销售实施新限制的消息首先出现在 Cyber​​Scoop 上。

【原文 English Original】
The Department of Commerce is rushing to put in place new export rules that prevent American companies from using third-party data center deals in other countries to evade restrictions on AI chip sales. On Monday, the Bureau of Industry and Security announced a 132-page interim final rule that limits the ability of American chipmakers to sell AI chips to third-party data centers abroad. The rule adds new restrictions on exports, reexports and transfers to overseas data centers in countries under U.S. arms embargoes. That list currently covers more than 20 nations, including China, Cuba, Iran, Libya, North Korea, and Sudan. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models,” the final interim rule states. “Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons [in those countries], as part of complying with this new control.” The rule also requires new licenses for sales of advanced AI chips to five other countries not on the arms embargo list: – Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has determined these countries present a “higher-than-normal risk” of chips being diverted to other parts of the world. Companies with pending or ongoing chip sales have 90 days to obtain the new licenses, which will contain fewer exemptions for overseas chip designers. The “interim final” designation allows Commerce to bypass much of the normal federal rulemaking process. According to the nonprofit American Action Forum, that designation is often reserved for “emergencies and other times of need.” Commerce cited its authority under the 2018 Export Control Reform Act to impose the changes without prior notice and comment. Lawmakers in the U.S. have consistently cited American dominance in the semiconductor industry as a key advantage over rivals like China, which is working to build out its own domestic AI chip industry. Some experts have urged the federal government to further tighten global sales of such chips to keep them from being diverted or purchased by hostile foreign powers. Placing AI chips on an arms embargo list reflects growing concern about the dangers AI systems bring in areas like hacking and bioweapon design. The rule was issued days after Jensen Huang, former CEO of American chip giant Nvidia, stepped down following reports of multiple affairs with staffers and a Chinese business associate. That associate, Alice Huang of Chinese company Megaspeed, is under scrutiny from U.S. policymakers as a potential Chinese government asset. Reports also say she helped broker $12 billion in deals between Megaspeed and Nvidia for AI chips, some of which may have been sent to China. title: China’s rare earth giants double profits as prices soar
zh_title: 价格飙升 中国稀土巨头利润翻倍
summary: 由于供应控制收紧和价格上涨加强了中国对全球制造业至关重要的市场的控制，中国最大的两家稀土生产商的利润在 2026 年前 9 个月增长了一倍多。中国最大的轻稀土公司中国北方稀土（CNRE）（上交所股票代码：600111）公布的第三季度业绩显示，净利润为人民币 36.5 亿元（合 5.472 亿美元）。专注于重稀土的中国稀土资源科技有限公司（SZSE：000831）今年前九个月的销售额增长了一倍多，达到 4.08 亿元人民币（约合 6110 亿美元）
content:
由于供应控制收紧和价格上涨加强了中国对全球制造业至关重要的市场的控制，中国最大的两家稀土生产商的利润在 2026 年前 9 个月增长了一倍多。中国最大的轻稀土公司中国北方稀土（CNRE）（上交所股票代码：600111）公布的第三季度业绩显示，净利润为人民币 36.5 亿元（合 5.472 亿美元）。专注于重稀土的中国稀土资源科技有限公司（SZSE：000831）今年前九个月的收入增长了一倍多，达到4.08亿元人民币（6110万美元）。花旗分析师王安娜对路透社表示：“供给侧改革通过改善行业纪律来帮助支撑价格。”盈利增长突显了北京遏制供应过剩和巩固生产的努力如何使国内生产商受益，同时增强了中国对战略矿产供应链的影响力。由于美国制造商仍然严重依赖中国稀土，这些管制措施还使习近平主席在与美国总统唐纳德·特朗普的贸易谈判中拥有影响力。轻稀土化合物钕镨 (NdPr) 的价格较首次实施管制时上涨了 62%，达到 719,000 元人民币（107,793 美元）。这两家公司是中国在 2024 年获得生产配额的唯一企业，当时中国的配额从之前的配额减少到了 6 家。
2025年，中国对稀土开采和加工实施了更严格的控制，将配额制度扩大到包括进口材料，并要求公司定期报告战略矿产的流动情况。中国将稀土控制范围扩大到进口材料。随着整合和政府战略的实施，两家公司的全年利润都将超出分析师的预期。中国的长期游戏在看到供应过剩对其他行业造成的影响后，中国采用了生产配额和整合来确保稀土不会成为另一个受害者。对国防、电池和磁铁至关重要的矿物类别很容易出现剧烈的价格波动，从而挤压了生产商的供应和利润。由于对国内生产的控制更加严格，并受到高需求和高价格的支撑，中国将其作为与其他强国谈判的筹码。中国的出口管制涵盖了几种利基中重稀土以及含有它们的磁体。随着特朗普和习近平本周再次会面，美国总统几乎没有空间对中国征收更多关税。尽管对该行业进行了数百万美元的投资，但美国的关键矿产项目仍然只停留在纸面上，距离投产还有数年时间。在习近平会谈之前，特朗普的矿产推动尚未放松中国的控制（路透社文件）

【原文 English Original】
China’s two largest rare earths producers more than doubled their profits in the first nine months of 2026 as tighter supply controls and rising prices strengthened the country’s grip on a market critical to global manufacturing.  The country’s biggest light rare earth firm, China Northern Rare Earth (CNRE) (SSE: 600111), reported net profit of 3.65 billion yuan ($547.2 million), based on third-quarter results.  China Rare Earth Resources and Technology (SZSE: 000831), which focuses on heavy rare earths, more than doubled through the first nine months of the year to 408 million yuan ($61.1 million).  “Supply-side reforms have helped support prices by improving industry discipline,” Citi analyst Anna Wang told Reuters .  The earnings gains highlight how Beijing’s efforts to curb oversupply and consolidate production are benefiting domestic producers while reinforcing China’s influence over strategic mineral supply chains. The controls also give President Xi Jinping leverage in trade negotiations with US President Donald Trump, as American manufacturers remain heavily dependent on Chinese rare earths.  Prices for light rare earth compound neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) are up 62% from when the controls were first introduced, to 719,000 yuan ($107,793).   The two companies were the only ones given production quotas by China in 2024, when the country downsized from giving quotas to six previously.  In 2025 China introduced tighter controls on the mining and processing of rare earths by extending the quota system to include imported materials and requiring companies to report on the flow of strategic minerals regularly. China extends rare earth controls to imported material With the consolidation and government strategies, both companies are set to beat analysts’ estimates for their full-year profit.  China’s long game   After seeing what oversupply can do to other industries, China has used production quotas and consolidation to make sure rare earths would not become another victim. The group of minerals critical for defence, batteries and magnets have been prone to aggressive price swings that have squeezed supply and profits for producers.  With a tighter grip on domestic production, and supported by high demand and prices, China uses that as leverage in negotiations with other powerful countries.   China’s export controls cover several niche medium and heavy rare earths and the magnets that contain them.  As Trump and Xi meet again this week, the American President will have little room for imposing more tariffs on China.   Even with multi-million dollar investments in the sector, critical minerals projects in the US are still only on paper, years away from production.  Trump’s minerals push has yet to loosen China’s grip ahead of Xi talks (With files from Reuters)

summary: 经过一周繁忙的发射活动，本周全球发射清单预计将进行六次发射，其中包括范登堡发射的 3 次 SpaceX 猎鹰 9 号发射任务、中国的两次发射任务以及南美洲的阿丽亚娜 6 号发射任务。 SpaceX 将为美国太空部队和国家侦察办公室发射有效载荷，而本周的中国任务和阿丽亚娜 6 号任务中至少有一次将发射一批互联网卫星。长征2D |有效载荷未知 11 月 18 日星期三，中国将发射长征 2D (CZ-2D) 火箭，预计将从 9 号发射场 (LC
content:
经过一周繁忙的发射活动，本周全球发射清单预计将进行六次发射，其中包括范登堡发射的 3 次 SpaceX 猎鹰 9 号发射任务、中国的两次发射任务以及南美洲的阿丽亚娜 6 号发射任务。 SpaceX 将为美国太空部队和国家侦察办公室发射有效载荷，而本周的中国任务和阿丽亚娜 6 号任务中至少有一次将发射一批互联网卫星。长征2D |有效载荷未知，将于 11 月 18 日星期三从中国发射，长征 2D (CZ-2D) 预计将于世界标准时间 22:50 从太原卫星发射中心的 9 号发射场 (LC-9) 发射。官方警告通知表明发射轨迹是向南的，但有效载荷及其预定轨道的详细信息要等到发射后才会发布。两级、40.77 米高的 CZ-2D 由上海航天技术研究院 (SAST) 制造。 2D 版本不需要额外的捆绑式助推器。此次飞行将是长征2D的第108次飞行，也是今年的第七次。猎鹰 9 号 | USSF-317 (R-6) SpaceX 将于 11 月 18 日星期三进行本周两次发射中的第一次发射，发射时间为四小时，发射窗口于太平洋标准时间晚上 7:00（世界标准时间周四 03:00）开始。
USSF-317 任务是美国太空军 (USSF) 本周的唯一任务，将从加利福尼亚州范登堡太空部队基地 (VSFB) 的东 4 号航天发射场 (SLC-4E) 发射，向东南飞行，将其机密有效载荷送入低地球轨道 (LEO)。所有系统看起来都很好，天气也有利于升空。猎鹰 9 号发射的 USSF-627 任务即将开始从加利福尼亚州发射推进剂 → https://t.co/IdlZbviZZl pic.twitter.com/fKxyN4DIui — SpaceX (@SpaceX) 2026 年 11 月 12 日助推器 B1100 将支持此次任务，这是自近一年前 11 月 23 日首次支持星链集团 11-30 以来的第十一次飞行， 2025 年。除了 NROL-105 和 USSF-385 之外，助推器之前的八次飞行支持了星链任务。 SpaceX 的西海岸无人机飞船 Of Course I Still Love You 将在 B1100 升空后约 8 分钟着陆时驻扎在地面。猎鹰 9 号是一枚直径 3.9 米、高 70 米的两级火箭。九台 Merlin 1D 发动机为第一级助推器提供动力，而第二级则使用一台真空优化的 Merlin 发动机。猎鹰 9 号和猎鹰重型火箭是第一批实现定期重复使用的轨道火箭，其中一枚猎鹰助推器已飞行 37 次。飞行后，两个有效载荷整流罩也被回收并重复使用。长征8A | SatNet LEO Group 本周的第二次中国发射计划于 11 月 11 日星期五举行。
世界标准时间 20 日 11:00，在中国文昌航天发射场的商业 LC-1 发射台上发射。长征 8A (CZ-8A) 将携带 9 颗通信卫星进入近地轨道，这些卫星由 SatNet 拥有并由中国卫星网络集团运营。 CZ-8A火箭有两个直径3.35米的级，总高度为50.54 m。第一级由两个捆绑式液体燃料助推器辅助。此次飞行将标志着 CZ-8A 的第 13 次飞行，也是 2026 年的第七次飞行。 NROL-136 SpaceX 本周的第二次猎鹰 9 号任务定于 11 月 21 日星期六太平洋标准时间凌晨 4:30（世界标准时间 12:30）发射，同样是从加州 VSFB 的 SLC-4E 发射。 NROL-136 任务将携带未知数量的有效载荷进入近地轨道，供国家侦察办公室 (NRO) 的增殖建筑星座使用，该星座由 Space 建造

【原文 English Original】
Following a week of busy launch activity, the worldwide launch manifest is set to see six launches this week, with three SpaceX Falcon 9 missions from Vandenberg, two Chinese missions, and an Ariane 6 mission from South America. SpaceX will launch payloads for the United States Space Force and the National Reconnaissance Office, while at least one of this week’s Chinese missions and the Ariane 6 will launch a batch of internet satellites. Chang Zheng 2D | Unknown Payload Wednesday, Nov. 18, will see a launch from China, with a Chang Zheng 2D (CZ-2D) expected to launch from Launch Complex 9 (LC-9) at the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center at 22:50 UTC. Official warning notices indicate a southerly launch trajectory, but details of the payload and its intended orbit will not be released until after launch. The two-stage, 40.77-m-tall CZ-2D is manufactured by the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology (SAST). The 2D variant requires no additional strap-on boosters. This flight will mark the 108th CZ-2D to fly, the seventh of this year. Falcon 9 | USSF-317 (R-6) SpaceX’s first of two launches this week comes on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at the start of a four-hour launch window that opens at 7:00 PM PST (03:00 UTC on Thursday). The only mission for the United States Space Force (USSF) this week, the USSF-317 mission will launch from Space Launch Complex 4 East (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base (VSFB) in California, flying southeast to place its classified payload into low-Earth orbit (LEO). All systems are looking good, and weather is favorable for liftoff. Propellant load is about to begin for Falcon 9’s launch of the USSF-627 mission from California → https://t.co/IdlZbviZZl pic.twitter.com/fKxyN4DIui — SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 12, 2026 Booster B1100 will support this mission, marking its eleventh flight since first supporting Starlink Group 11-30 nearly a year ago on Nov. 23, 2025. Eight of the booster’s previous flights supported Starlink missions, in addition to flying NROL-105 and USSF-385. SpaceX’s west coast droneship, Of Course I Still Love You, will be stationed downrange for B1100’s landing approximately eight minutes after liftoff. Falcon 9 is a 3.9-m-diameter, 70-m-tall two-stage rocket. Nine Merlin 1D engines power the first-stage booster, while the second stage uses a single vacuum-optimized Merlin engine. Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy were the first orbital rockets to achieve regular re-use, with one Falcon booster having flown 37 flights. The two payload fairings are also recovered and reused after flight. Chang Zheng 8A | SatNet LEO Group The second Chinese launch of the week is scheduled for Friday, Nov. 20, at 11:00 UTC from the Commercial LC-1 pad at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China. A Chang Zheng 8A (CZ-8A) will carry nine communications satellites into LEO, with the satellites owned by SatNet and operated by the China Satellite Network Group. The CZ-8A rocket features two 3.35-m-diameter stages, with a total height of 50.54 m. The first stage is assisted by two strap-on liquid-fuelled boosters. This flight will mark the 13th overall CZ-8A flight, the seventh of 2026. Falcon 9 | NROL-136 SpaceX’s second Falcon 9 mission of the week is scheduled to launch on Saturday, Nov. 21, at 4:30 AM PST (12:30 UTC), again from SLC-4E at VSFB in California. The NROL-136 mission will carry an unknown number of payloads into LEO for the National Reconnaissance Office’s (NRO) Proliferated Architecture constellation, built by SpaceX and Northrop Grumman. The booster supporting this mission will be B1097, flying for the 14th time. This booster first flew on Sept. 3, 2025, and has previously flown eight Starlink missions, as well as NROL-172, Transporter 17, Sentinel-6B, Twilight (Pandora & Others), and USSF-259. Following stage separation, B1097 will conduct a return-to-launch-site landing at Landing Zone 4 (LZ-4), located directly next to SLC-4E. Ariane 64 | Amazon Leo (LE-04) Amazon is continuing to put together its constellation of Leo satellites and will add another 36 on Monday, Nov. 23, at 10:12 UTC aboard an Ariane 64. The rocket will launch from Ensemble de Lancement Ariane 4 (ELA-4) at the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana, with the launch window lasting five hours and 27 minutes. Ariane 64 will follow a northeastern trajectory, delivering 22,000 kg of Leo satellites into LEO. Ariane 64 is a 62-m-tall, 5.4-m-diameter, expendable two-stage rocket built by the ArianeGroup on behalf of the European Space Agency. Both stages are powered by liquid hydrogen and oxygen-fuelled engines. The 64 variant of the basic Ariane 6 utilizes four P129 strap-on solid rocket boosters to provide additional lift-off thrust. This will be the fifth Ariane 6 mission of 2026. Watch the full replay of #VA269 . Relive Ariane 6's successful mission carrying 36 Amazon Leo satellites into orbit. First flight with P160C boosters Heaviest Ariane payload ever #LaunchingAmbitions #Ariane6 #VA269 @Amazonleo @ArianeGroup @esa @CNES @EuropeSpacePort pic.twitter.com/YLxW60wAo1 — Arianespace (@Arianespace) June 17, 2026 Falcon 9 | USSF-266 (TH-3) Closing out the week, a Falcon 9 launch is currently scheduled for Monday, Nov. 23, at 8:04 AM PST (16:04 UTC) — the third this week from SLC-4E at VSFB. The classified USSF-266 mission has a four-hour launch window extending to 12:04 PM PST (20:04 UTC). Falcon 9 will fly due south, indicating a polar orbit for the payload. While the payload is classified, the launch trajectory and other factors suggest that this may be an additional batch of satellites for the USSF’s Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator (SB-AMTI) program. These are based on the SpaceX Starshield satellite bus. The Falcon 9 booster supporting this flight will be B1081, making its 29th flight. B1081 first flew on Aug. 26, 2023, and flew four missions from SpaceX’s Florida launch sites before moving to Vandenberg for Transporter 10, where it has operated since then. The booster will land atop Of Course I Still Love You , stationed approximately 640 km downrange in the Pacific Ocean. If the current schedule holds, this will mark the 122nd Falcon 9 flight of 2026, and the 273rd orbital launch attempt worldwide in 2026. (Lead Image: Falcon 9 launches into the Florida morning skies. content:
整理经济动力产业：分析研究和政策建议选集|书籍和编辑卷| 2026 年 11 月 16 日 | ITIF跳到内容
整理经济动力产业：分析研究和政策建议选集
中国主导战略重要产业的系统性运动如何威胁美国的技术领先地位、经济实力和国家安全，以及美国政策制定者应该采取什么措施。
信息技术与创新基金会 (ITIF) 进行了为期 18 个月的研究，探讨中国霸道的产业战略如何威胁美国的技术领先地位、经济实力和国家安全。 ITIF 的研究得出的结论是，美国政策制定者必须从根本上改变该国的科技工业经济体系，以防止美国在为 21 世纪国家实力提供基础的关键先进贸易部门行业中屈服于中国。 ITIF 将这些行业称为“国民经济动力行业”。
这项研究工作于 2025 年 11 月至 2026 年 11 月期间产生了一系列 19 份政策报告。
该系列的第一份报告全面概述了中国正在发动的技术经济贸易战，以牺牲美国及其西方盟友的利益来主导这些行业。
第二组九份报告包括对美国工业表现与中国在国民经济实力行业方面的定量和定性分析。
第三组共九份报告，为美国政策制定者提供了近 200 条具体建议，以重组政府并动员起来应对与中国的技术经济贸易战。
这些报告可以连续提供，也可以作为选集提供：
随后是概述报告的执行摘要以及 ITIF 政策建议索引。
中国正在系统性地主导先进产业，从而在 21 世纪增强国家实力，美国面临着生存挑战。与美国历史上的任何竞争对手不同，中国将拥有 14 亿人口的大陆经济规模与明确致力于实现对西方民主世界的技术经济优势的马克思列宁主义政治体系结合起来。这不是市场经济体之间的正常经济竞争，而是一场精心策划的、长达数十年的战略运动，旨在取代美国的工业能力、削弱盟国，并从根本上重塑中共领导下的全球秩序。
其中的利害关系超越了经济范畴。今天的国家实力取决于本报告所称的“国家电力工业”的实力，这些部门涵盖纯粹的国防生产、军事和商业应用中使用的军民两用技术，以及支持更广泛工业公域的赋能产业。其中包括半导体、航空航天、生物制药、电信设备、先进化学品、精密机械、机器人、人工智能（AI）系统以及其他数十个领域，在这些领域，企业实力减弱或受到致命伤害将赋予中国对美国及其盟国的危险影响力，并削弱美国的国防生产能力。
按照目前的发展轨迹，中国很可能很快就会在国家电力行业积累比美国大得多的能力。
本次比赛的对手是 bac

【原文 English Original】
Marshaling Economic Power Industries: An Anthology of Analytical Research and Policy Recommendations | Books & Edited Volumes | Nov 16, 2026 | ITIFSkip to content
Marshaling Economic Power Industries: An Anthology of Analytical Research and Policy Recommendations
How China’s systematic campaign to dominate strategically important industries threatens America’s technological leadership, economic strength, and national security—and what U.S. policymakers should do about it.
The Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF) has conducted an 18-month research effort examining how China’s domineering industrial strategy threatens U.S. technological leadership, economic strength, and national security. ITIF’s research concludes that U.S. policymakers must fundamentally transform the country’s techno-industrial economic system to prevent America from becoming subservient to China in a critical group of advanced, traded-sector industries that provide the foundation for national power in the 21st century. ITIF calls these industries “national economic power industries.”
This research effort produced a series of 19 policy reports from November 2025 through November 2026.
The first report in the series provides a comprehensive overview of the unfolding techno-economic-trade war that China is waging to dominate these industries at the expense of the United States and its allies in the West.
A second group of nine reports includes quantitative and qualitative analyses of U.S. industrial performance versus China in national economic power industries.
A third group of nine reports offers nearly 200 specific recommendations for U.S. policymakers to reorganize government and mobilize for the techno-economic-trade war with China.
The reports are available both serially and as an anthology:
An executive summary of the overview report follows, along with an index of ITIF’s policy recommendations.
The United States faces an existential challenge in China’s systematic campaign to dominate the advanced industries that enable national power in the 21st century. Unlike any competitor in American history, China combines the continental scale of a 1.4-billion-person economy with a Marxist-Leninist political system explicitly committed to achieving techno-economic supremacy over the Western democratic world. This is not normal economic competition between market economies—it is a carefully orchestrated, multi-decade strategic campaign to displace U.S. industrial capabilities, weaken allied nations, and fundamentally reshape the global order under CCP leadership.
The stakes transcend economics. National power today depends on strength in what this report terms “national power industries”—a spectrum of sectors spanning pure defense production, dual-use technologies employed in both military and commercial applications, and enabling industries that support the broader industrial commons. These include semiconductors, aerospace, biopharmaceuticals, telecommunications equipment, advanced chemicals, precision machinery, robotics, artificial intelligence (AI) systems, and dozens of other sectors in which weakened or fatally injured firms would grant China dangerous leverage over the United States and its allies, as well as weaken U.S. defense production capabilities.
On its current trajectory, it is likely that China will soon amass significantly greater capabilities than the United States will in national power industries.
This competition occurs against a backdrop of American policy failure. For over two decades, U.S. leaders across both parties have operated under the assumption that China was becoming a “normal” market economy that would gradually liberalize politically and economically. That assumption has proven catastrophically wrong. China today is more authoritarian, more aggressive internationally, and more committed to state-directed capitalism than at any point since Mao’s death.
On its current trajectory, it is likely that China will soon amass significantly greater capabilities than the United States will in national power industries. With those greater capabilities will come geostrategic hegemony over the West, unless the United States forestalls that outcome by adopting a new, transformative national power industry strategy that goes beyond a mere competitiveness or national innovation strategy. This is not a war that the United States and allies can win in the sense of significantly weakening or retarding the growth of China’s own national power industries. The only way Chinese attacks will end is if China becomes a free, democratic country. But the United States and allies can avoid defeat—keeping their national power industries relatively strong—by working together and adopting national power industry strategies.
Understanding the Chinese Communist Party’s True Objectives
Perhaps the most damning evidence of Chinese intentions comes from internal Communist Party documents and speeches intended for party members rather than foreign audiences. As China scholar Daniel Tobin has documented, these reveal a regime explicitly committed to Marxist-Leninist global ambitions that go far beyond merely moving up the value chain and growing its economy.
Xi Jinping has repeatedly framed China’s rise in ideological terms, stating that “scientific socialism is full of vitality in 21st century China” and that China offers “a new option for other countries and nations who want to speed up their development while preserving their independence.” In a 2013 speech to senior party officials, Xi declared that “the viewpoint of historical materialism that capitalism is doomed to failure and socialism will prevail” remains valid, and that China must “seize the initiative, win the competitive edge, and secure our future” in a “long-term cooperation and rivalry between the two social systems.”
Documents from the party’s 20th Congress state that China’s success has “significantly shifted the worldwide historical evolution of the contest between the two different ideologies and social systems of socialism and capitalism in a way that favors socialism.” Chinese leaders explicitly describe their work as part of a “great struggle” and “systems contest with Western capitalist democracy,” using terminology that leaves no ambiguity about their intentions.
On technology and industry specifically, party documents are equally explicit. The minister of Science and Technology wrote in the People’s Daily that “the scientific and technological revolution and the contest between major powers are intertwined; the high-tech field has become the forefront and main battlefield of international competition.” Another official commentary stated: “To a certain extent, those who gain access to the Internet will gain the world. Core technology is an important weapon for the country.”
China’s Made in China 2025 plan, while officially downplayed after international backlash, clearly articulates the goal: “Building an internationally competitive manufacturing industry is the only way China can enhance its comprehensive national strength, ensure national security, and build itself into a world power.” The plan calls for China to “seize the commanding heights of a new round of competition in the manufacturing industry” and achieve innovation leadership “ranking first globally.”
The CCP follows a predictable playbook across industry after industry.
Leading Chinese scholar Lu Yongxiang stated in 2024 that “by 2035, ‘Made in China’ will surpass the United States and become the global leader,” noting this would thrust the world into a “new era”—explicitly referencing an era of Chinese dominance. These are not the words of a nation seeking merely to “catch up” or achieve “legitimate development.” They are the explicit articulation of a campaign for global advanced industrial hegemony.
China’s actions match its rhetoric. The CCP follows a predictable playbook across industry after industry. First, attract foreign investment by promising market access. Second, coerce technology transfer through joint venture requirements and other mechanisms—pressure the U.S. Trade Representative has characterized as “particularly intense.” Third, support domestic firms in copying and incorporating foreign technology while building indigenous capabilities through programs such as the 2006 Medium- and Long-term Program for Science and Technology Development, which identified 402 core technologies to master.
Fourth, carve out and protect the Chinese market for Chinese firms, excluding foreign competitors once domestic champions can reasonably serve the entire Chinese market. Fifth, provide massive subsidies—estimated at minimum 1.73 percent of Chinese gross domestic product (GDP) annually, or over $400 billion per year, though actual figures are likely far higher accounting for provincial and local support. Finally, support Chinese firms “going out” to capture global market share, particularly in developing nations through Belt and Road Initiative investments exceeding $1 trillion. These dwarf the minimal industrial subsidies the U.S. government (USG) provides.
The scale of Chinese subsidies dwarfs anything in Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) nations. A German institute found that in 2022, 99 percent of listed Chinese firms received direct government subsidies, with electric vehicle (EV) maker BYD alone receiving over $3.7 billion. Chinese industrial subsidies were 4.5 times greater than U.S. subsidies as a share of GDP. Combined with a chronically undervalued currency, suppressed domestic consumption, and closed markets, these subsidies have enabled Chinese firms to sell below cost for years or decades, systematically destroying foreign competitors’ market positions.
This is not to say that all Chinese efforts or innovation are win-lose. If China invents a cure for Alzheimer’s, the world benefits (assuming the United States or its allies would not also do so). But this would also reduce U.S. (and allied) strength in the pharmaceutical industry.
Overall, the policy debate about China is largely dominated by international relations scholars and experts, not business or industrial strategy experts. The former are aware of the global competition for leadership in advanced industries, but they largely see it as subservient to overall foreign policy considerations and goals. Moreover, few understand the operation of advanced industries, the nature of the competition, or the importance of barriers to entry and reentry. As such, the prevailing narratives largely ignore techno-economic and trade war implications and the implications for U.S. power.
Current U.S. thinking about China coalesces around three main strategic approaches, all of which are inadequate to the challenge.
The first camp, still influential in much of the U.S. foreign policy establishment, prioritizes maintaining cooperative relations with China, even in the face of CCP behavior that harms U.S. national power industry capabilities. These experts argue that China’s growth benefits global prosperity, that Chinese cooperation is essential for addressing climate change and other global challenges, and that confrontation risks becoming a catastrophic conflict.
A 2019 open letter signed by over 100 prominent scholars claimed that “we do not believe Beijing is an economic enemy or an existential national security threat” and argued that “the fear that Beijing will replace the United States as the global leader is exaggerated.”
This camp consistently minimizes Chinese malfeasance while emphasizing supposed benefits of engagement. They cite Chinese economic growth as driving global prosperity (ignoring that China’s persistent trade surpluses actually reduce GDP elsewhere). In arguing that cooperation is needed on issues such as climate change, pandemic response, and AI governance, they gloss over the question of why the United States should be the supplicant when China has equal or greater interest in addressing these challenges.
Their fundamental error is treating China as a partner rather than a strategic competitor. Engagers assume that continued dialogue and economic ties will moderate China’s behavior, when two decades of evidence proves otherwise. They prioritize the process of engagement over the substance of outcomes, accepting Chinese predatory practices as the price of maintaining access and conversation.
The Deniers: Wait for China’s Collapse or Assume Inherent U.S. Superiority
A second camp acknowledges China’s rise but counsels patience, predicting that internal contradictions will lead to Chinese economic stagnation or political crisis. These analysts point to demographic decline, the housing bubble, government debt, and the inefficiencies of state capitalism as harbingers of inevitable Chinese failure. To be sure, many advance the well-trodden prescriptions such as improved K-12 education, more high-skill immigration, smarter regulation, and more government spending on science. But they will not go so far as to support a national power industry strategy.
This “Peak China” thesis is seductive because it requires no painful U.S. policy changes. If China is destined to collapse under its own weight, the United States need only wait and maintain its existing approaches to the economy, trade, and national security. Proponents cite any negative Chinese economic news as evidence that their predictions are materializing, while ignoring continued Chinese gains in technological capabilities and global market share of advanced industries.
The fatal flaw is mistaking China for the Soviet Union. Unlike Soviet command economics, Chinese state capitalism has proven remarkably effective at generating growth and technological advancement. The CCP studied why the Soviet Union failed and adopted fundamentally different economic management—allowing market forces to operate within state-directed strategic frameworks rather than attempting to centrally plan everything.
Moreover, even if China faces economic headwinds from demographics or debt, these business-cycle challenges do not negate its structural advantages in the techno-economic competition. Chinese firms will continue benefiting from massive subsidies, protected markets, and patient capital regardless of GDP growth rates. Waiting for China to self-destruct while Chinese companies dismantle Western industries one after another is a prescription for defeat.
The Innovationists: Technology Will Save Us
The third camp acknowledges the challenge China presents but argues that American innovation superiority will enable the United States to prevail. These “dynamists” focus on deregulation, immigration reform, scientific research funding, and nurturing entrepreneurship—particularly in cutting-edge fields such as AI, quantum computing, and synthetic biology.
This view holds that the United States need not defend legacy industries because American innovators will create entirely new sectors and the United States will lead them. Why fight over solar panels or EVs when we can dominate AI and quantum? The prescription is to boost science funding, reduce regulatory barriers, import more STEM (science, technology, engineering, and math) talent, and trust that Silicon Valley-style innovation will deliver victory.
The problems with this strategy are multiple. First, with a few exceptions (e.g., AI), it is industry-agnostic—there is no guarantee that market-driven innovation will produce capabilities in sectors that matter most for national power. Second, the United States has repeatedly lost production of technologies it invented, from televisions to solar panels to batteries, as other nations have commercialized American discoveries. Innovation alone does not ensure domestic production or competitive strength.
Third, advanced defense systems increasingly rely on commercial technologies (spin-on rather than spin-off), making a strategy that abandons commercial sectors to China while hoping to maintain defense-only production unrealistic and prohibitively expensive. Fourth, the “industrial commons”—the ecosystem of suppliers, skilled workers, and manufacturing capabilities—erodes when industries disappear, making future innovation harder. Intel founder Andy Grove’s warning resonates: “Abandoning today’s ‘commodity’ manufacturing can lock you out of tomorrow’s emerging industry.”
Finally, China is not ceding emerging technologies. Chinese firms are competitive or leading in AI (see Alibaba, Baidu, and DeepSeek), quantum communications, commercial space, robotics, and biotechnology. The notion that the United States can retreat to “higher ground” in emerging tech while China dominates established industries ignores that Chinese firms are aggressively pursuing both.
Why Current U.S. Economic Policy Frameworks Fail
The deeper problem is that dominant U.S. economic doctrines are fundamentally mismatched to the era of national power industry competition.
The reigning paradigm in U.S. economic policymaking—which critics call “neoliberalism”—treats all industries as equivalent. Financial services and semiconductor fabrication are no different; both simply respond to market signals. The goal is to maximize consumer welfare through efficient resource allocation, which markets achieve better than governments do.
In this framework, Chinese subsidies (including low labor costs and lax environmental regulations) are gifts to American consumers (lower prices!), not strategic attacks. Trade deficits reflect American prosperity (we’re rich enough to buy foreign goods!), not industrial weakness. Offshoring production to China demonstrates smart capital allocation by U.S. firms seeking higher returns, not a national security vulnerability.
The reigning paradigm in U.S. economic policymaking—which critics call “neoliberalism”—treats all industries as equivalent.
Consumer welfare economics has no concept of strategic industries or national power. Its proponents argue that “countries don’t compete, only companies do” and that concerns about industrial structure reflect economically illiterate protectionism. The Peterson Institute epitomizes this view, arguing that U.S.-China trade is “clearly win-win” and that “Chinese companies have a right to compete with U.S. companies and succeed in any sector, including in high-tech.”
This doctrine might have been adequate when America faced no serious techno-economic competitor; it is catastrophically inadequate against China’s state capitalist predation. Markets have no inherent reason to preserve semiconductor fabrication, aerospace, or pharmaceutical production domestically. They are equally happy producing legal services, retail, and hospitality, none of which enable national power.
But the reality of this techno-economic and trade attack fundamentally undercuts the foundation of consumer welfare economics and exposes its inability to address the current challenge. If national power is the ultimate goal, not consumer welfare, then this doctrine fails, at least in guiding the share of the economy composed of national economic power industries. If a nation’s industrial mix is critical, then a doctrine that gives equal weight to potato chips and computer chips fails.
The ascendant alternative on the Left is equally unsuited to the challenge. Neo–New Dealism focuses on redistribution, social justice, and worker welfare overgrowth and competitiveness. Its industrial policy priorities are human services (childcare, eldercare), climate-focused sectors (renewable energy), and breaking up large corporations through aggressive antitrust.
While rhetorically supporting “industrial policy,” progressives’ actual agenda—drug price controls, restricting intellectual property (IP), mandating labor standards that limit automation, attacking profitable corporations as exploitative—systematically weakens the large advanced-technology firms that must serve as national champions against Chinese competitors.
Moreover, neo–New Dealism’s massive social spending agenda would consume the fiscal resources needed for strategic industrial investment. Its anticorporate ideology and deep suspicion of business-government collaboration make the public-private partnerships required for an effective national power industry strategy politically toxic.
The reality of the CCP’s techno-economic and trade war on the West undercuts the foundations of neo–New Deal progressivism. If the United States is in an existential contest for global power, then boosting taxes and regulations on business is especially ill-advised, as are the neo-Brandeisian campaign to destroy large corporations and separate unrestrained demands from organized labor. Progressive advocates know this quite well, which is why they go to any end to deny that China is even a competitor.
What’s Required: National Power Industry Strategy
The United States needs a fundamentally new framework: a national power industry strategy. This approach recognizes the following:
Industries differ fundamentally in strategic importance. Semiconductors and furniture are not equivalent. Some sectors—defense, dual-use, and enabling—are critical to national power and must be prioritized even at short-term economic cost.
Markets are indifferent to national power. Unregulated market forces will not automatically preserve strategic capabilities. Government must actively shape industrial structure through strategy, not just generic competitiveness or innovation policies.
China is a strategic competitor, not a normal trading partner. Chinese mercantilism requires defensive measures (restricting imports produced unfairly) and offensive support (strengthening domestic champions in national power industries) that violate free-market and progressive orthodoxies.
Production matters as much as innovation. The United States cannot rely on inventing technologies that China then produces. Manufacturing capabilities, supply chain resilience, and industrial commons must be preserved domestically in strategic sectors.
Long-term strategic positioning trumps short-term efficiency. Maintaining redundant capacity, subsidizing strategic industries, and accepting higher consumer prices are necessary costs of not losing the techno-economic war.
This requires jettisoning the deeply held view that governments should not “pick winners.” Markets might optimize GDP growth, but only by happenstance will this generate needed national power industry capabilities. Policymakers must embrace strategic industry selection and support, drawing on business strategy frameworks rather than consumer welfare economics.
The political economy obstacles to a national power industry strategy are severe. U.S. business leaders, shaped by decades of financial capitalism prioritizing quarterly returns and shareholder value, distrust government involvement and focus myopically on firm-level profitability rather than systemic strength. Unlike their predecessors from the 1940s–1970s who saw themselves as corporate statesmen with responsibilities to the broader capitalist system, today’s executives view government industrial policy as either incompetent interference or the thin edge of socialist control.
Labor unions pursue short-term wage gains that often undermine firms’ long-term global competitiveness because they are unable to escape the prisoner’s dilemma of aggressive bargaining today leading to job losses to less-constrained Chinese rivals tomorrow.
Conservative organizations reflexively oppose the government activism required for industrial strategy, while progressive organizations reflexively oppose supporting corporations. Neither party’s dominant coalition supports the combination of strong state capacity and empowered corporate champions that a national power industry strategy requires.
Perhaps most critically, the USG itself lacks the analytical capacity, institutional structures, and personnel with expertise to formulate and execute sophisticated industrial strategy. Unlike China, where officials study industrial policy as a discipline and spend careers mastering sectoral dynamics, U.S. policymakers typically have backgrounds in law or generalist economics divorced from operational understanding of specific industries and technologies.
The United States requires political, policy, and institutional transformation comparable to previous pivots after the War of 1812, the Civil War, and World War II. In all three cases, war provided the spur to overcome inertia and interest group resistance. We certainly hope it will not take a physical war to achieve similar transformation today. Either way, the organizing principle of economic policy must shift from maximizing consumer welfare or spurring social justice to ensuring that the United States maintains superior capabilities in national power industries relative to China. The simplest measures of this are the share of these industries’ global output that is produced in the United States and the share of U.S. production that occurs in allied nations. Related measures are the technological sophistication of U.S. products and services in national power industries compared with those of Chinese competitors.
The United States requires political, policy, and institutional transformation comparable to previous pivots after the War of 1812, the Civil War, and World War II.
This demands classifying industries by strategic importance, developing sophisticated strategies for priority sectors informed by business strategy principles rather than economics, restricting unfairly traded Chinese goods’ access to allied markets, substantially increasing public and private investment in strategic sectors (on the order of $100 billion per year in tax incentives and direct expenditures for at least a decade), coordinating with allies to present unified responses, and building government institutional capacity for industrial strategy.
The costs will be significant: Implementing a national power industry strategy will bring higher prices for certain consumer goods, increased government spending, greater fiscal discipline elsewhere, and reduced returns for some investors as capital is channeled toward strategic rather than merely profitable uses. But the alternative is worse: a future in which Chinese dominance of advanced industries leaves the United States dependent on an adversary for critical technologies, unable to defend its interests or protect its allies, and relegated to second-tier status in a China-dominated world order.
History shows that America can make fundamental pivots when circumstances demand. Whether it can do so absent the shock of military conflict—which might come too late, after critical capabilities are already lost—remains the defining question of our era. The window for effective action is narrowing. Chinese positions in industry after industry are becoming entrenched, protected by economies of scale, learning curves, network effects, and the enormous barriers to reentry that characterize advanced manufacturing. The reality is that once advanced industry capabilities are lost, they are extremely difficult to resurrect.
The choice facing America is stark and unavoidable: Fundamentally reform techno-economic policy now by embracing the uncomfortable truth that some industries matter far more than others—and by recognizing that preserving them requires active government strategy—or accept a managed decline into second-tier status while China’s techno-economic dominance translates into geopolitical supremacy. There is no third option, no magical innovation breakthrough that will solve the problem without hard choices and real sacrifices.
The United States remains far stronger than any declining power in history. Its advantages in innovation ecosystems, allied networks, capital markets, universities, and democratic legitimacy provide a foundation for successful competition if properly mobilized. But time is not on America’s side. Every industry lost makes recovery harder; every year of Chinese industrial expansion shifts the balance further; every failure to act because it violates free-market or progressive orthodoxies surrenders ground that cannot be regained. The techno-economic war with China is the central challenge of the 21st century. America’s response will determine not just its own future but the future of the liberal democratic world.
